# Threshold, output power and photon lifetime {#sec-threshold} [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/{{< var github_user >}}/{{< var repo >}}/blob/main/{{< var subdir >}}/notebooks/threshold.ipynb){.colab-link}  Run this chapter's code in Google Colab (no installation). *Slides 63–68 (gain coefficient and population inversion, threshold gain, phase condition, output versus pump rate), 69 and 74 (threshold inversion of the He–Ne laser), 70–73 (output power and photon cavity lifetime). Also the two exercises of the course MATLAB live script `Chapter4.mlx`.* ## Key relations The gain coefficient is the fractional power increase per unit length (slide 64). Writing the net stimulated emission rate $(N_2-N_1)B_{21}\rho$ with $\rho\approx N_\text{ph}h\nu_0/\Delta\nu$ gives the peak gain in terms of the inversion, $$ g(\nu_0)\approx(N_2-N_1)\frac{B_{21}nh\nu_0}{c\,\Delta\nu}. $$ A wave that makes one round trip in a cavity of length $L$, with mirror reflectances $R_1$, $R_2$ and internal loss $\alpha_s$, returns with the power $P_f=P_iR_1R_2e^{2gL}e^{-2\alpha_sL}$. Steady oscillation needs $P_f=P_i$ (slide 65): the gain must equal the total loss, $$ g_{th}=\alpha_t=\alpha_s+\frac{1}{2L}\ln\frac{1}{R_1R_2}. $$ The phase must also repeat after a round trip, $nk_m\,2L=2\pi m$ (slide 67), which selects the longitudinal modes of @sec-gas. With $A_{21}/B_{21}$ from @sec-einstein, the threshold inversion is (slide 66) $$ (N_2-N_1)_{th}\approx g_{th}\frac{8\pi n^2\nu_0^2\tau_{sp}\Delta\nu}{c^2}. $$ Photons leave the cavity through the mirrors and are absorbed inside it. The photon population decays with the **photon cavity lifetime** (slide 72) and the output power is the photon flux through mirror 1 (slide 71): $$ \tau_{ph}=\frac{2nL}{c\left[1-e^{-2\alpha_tL}\right]}\approx\frac{n}{c\,\alpha_t},\qquad P_o=\tfrac12A(1-R_1)h\nu_0N_\text{ph}\frac{c}{n}. $$ Above threshold the inversion is **clamped** at $(N_2-N_1)_{th}$. Every extra pump excitation becomes a stimulated photon, so $P_o$ grows linearly with the pump rate (slide 68). ## Threshold calculator ```{ojs} //| echo: false presets = ({ "He–Ne (slides 69, 73)": {L: 40, R1: 0.95, R2: 1.0, as: 0.05, n: 1.0, lam: 632.8, dnu: 1.5e9, tsp: 100e-9, d: 0.8}, "Nd:YAG rod": {L: 10, R1: 0.90, R2: 0.999, as: 0.3, n: 1.82, lam: 1064, dnu: 120e9, tsp: 230e-6, d: 4}, "GaAs laser diode (slide 131)": {L: 0.025, R1: 0.32, R2: 0.32, as: 1000, n: 3.6, lam: 860, dnu: 8e12, tsp: 2.5e-9, d: 0.002}, "InGaAsP FP diode, one HR facet":{L: 0.03, R1: 0.30, R2: 0.90, as: 1500, n: 3.5, lam: 1550, dnu: 5e12, tsp: 2e-9, d: 0.002} }) viewof preset = Inputs.select(Object.keys(presets), {label: "start from"}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof th = { const p = presets[preset]; return Inputs.form({ L: Inputs.number({value: p.L, label: "cavity length L (cm)"}), R1: Inputs.range([0.01, 0.9999], {value: p.R1, step: 0.0001, label: "output mirror R₁"}), R2: Inputs.range([0.01, 1], {value: p.R2, step: 0.0001, label: "back mirror R₂"}), as: Inputs.number({value: p.as, label: "internal loss α_s (m⁻¹)"}), n: Inputs.number({value: p.n, label: "refractive index n"}), lam: Inputs.number({value: p.lam, label: "wavelength λ₀ (nm)"}), dnu: Inputs.number({value: p.dnu, label: "gain linewidth Δν (Hz)"}), tsp: Inputs.number({value: p.tsp, label: "spontaneous lifetime τ_sp (s)"}) }); } ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false thOut = { const c = 299792458, L = th.L*1e-2, nu = c/(th.lam*1e-9); const mir = Math.log(1/(th.R1*th.R2))/(2*L), at = th.as + mir; const tph = 2*th.n*L/(c*(1 - Math.exp(-2*at*L))), tph0 = th.n/(c*at); const dN = at*8*Math.PI*th.n**2*nu**2*th.tsp*th.dnu/c**2; const fsr = c/(2*th.n*L), dnuc = 1/(2*Math.PI*tph), Q = 2*Math.PI*nu*tph; return {at, mir, tph, tph0, dN, fsr, dnuc, Q, F: fsr/dnuc, ee: Math.log(1/th.R1)/(2*L)/at}; } html`

The laser diode has an enormous loss (55 cm⁻¹), mostly through its 32 % cleaved facets, and compensates with an enormous gain. Its photon lifetime is picoseconds, which is what makes GHz modulation possible (@sec-modulation). ## Worked examples (slides 69 and 73), recomputed > He–Ne laser at 632.8 nm ($\nu_0=473.8$ THz), $L=40$ cm, $R_1=0.95$, $R_2=1$, $\Delta\nu=1.5$ GHz, $\alpha_s=0.05$ m⁻¹, > $\tau_{sp}=100$ ns, $n=1$. Find the threshold gain and inversion. With a 0.8 mm tube and 2.5 mW output, find the photon > lifetime and the photon concentration. ::: {#tbl-hene-th .cell tbl-cap='Slides 69 and 73 recomputed.' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} gth = lz.threshold_gain(0.05, 0.40, 0.95, 1.0) dN = lz.threshold_inversion(gth, 473.8e12, 100e-9, 1.5e9) tph, tph0 = lz.photon_lifetime(gth, 0.40), lz.photon_lifetime(gth, 0.40, exact=False) Nph = 2.5e-3/lz.gas_laser_output(1.0, np.pi*(0.4e-3)**2, 0.95, 474e12) pd.DataFrame([("threshold gain g_th = α_t", f"{gth:.3f} m⁻¹", "0.114 m⁻¹"), ("threshold inversion (N₂ − N₁)_th", f"{dN:.2e} m⁻³", "≈ 1.1×10¹⁵ m⁻³"), ("photon lifetime, exact (4.6.12)", f"{tph*1e9:.1f} ns", "30.6 ns"), ("photon lifetime, n/(cα_t) (4.6.13)", f"{tph0*1e9:.1f} ns", "29.2 ns"), ("photon concentration N_ph", f"{Nph:.2e} m⁻³", "2.1×10¹⁵ m⁻³")], columns=["quantity", "computed", "slide"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Only about $10^{15}$ inverted Ne atoms per m³ are needed, a fraction $10^{-7}$ of the gas: gas lasers work with tiny inversions spread over large volumes. ## The Fabry–Perot resonator: exercises of `Chapter4.mlx` The MATLAB live script of the course contains two exercises on Fabry–Perot cavities in semiconductor lasers. > **Exercise 1.** InGaAsP–InP FP laser, $L=250$ µm, peak at 1550 nm, $n=3.8$, $\alpha_s=20$ cm⁻¹, gain FWHM 2 nm. Find the > mode number, the mode spacing, the number of modes and the facet reflectance. > > **Exercise 2.** Semiconductor FP cavity, $L=200$ µm, $n=3.6$. Find the mode nearest to 1300 nm, the mode separation and the > spectral width of each mode for $R=0.9$ and $0.8$. ::: {#tbl-mlx .cell tbl-cap='The two exercises of Chapter4.mlx. The spectral width of a passive cavity mode is Δν_m/F with the finesse F = π√R/(1 − R).' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} R = lz.facet_R(3.8); m1 = lz.mode_number(250e-6, 1550e-9, 3.8) dnu1, dl1 = lz.mode_spacing(250e-6, 1550e-9, 3.8) m2 = lz.mode_number(200e-6, 1300e-9, 3.6); dnu2, dl2 = lz.mode_spacing(200e-6, 1300e-9, 3.6) rows = [("Ex. 1: facet reflectance ((n − 1)/(n + 1))²", f"{R:.3f}"), ("Ex. 1: mode number m = 2nL/λ", f"{m1:.1f} → {round(m1)}"), ("Ex. 1: mode spacing", f"{dnu1/1e9:.1f} GHz = {dl1*1e9:.3f} nm"), ("Ex. 1: modes in 2 nm", f"{2/(dl1*1e9):.2f} → 2 or 3 modes"), ("Ex. 1: threshold gain with α_s = 20 cm⁻¹", f"{lz.threshold_gain(2000, 250e-6, R)/100:.1f} cm⁻¹"), ("Ex. 2: mode number nearest 1300 nm", f"{m2:.1f} → {round(m2)} (λ = {2*3.6*200e-6/round(m2)*1e9:.2f} nm)"), ("Ex. 2: mode spacing", f"{dnu2/1e9:.1f} GHz = {dl2*1e9:.3f} nm")] for Rm in (0.9, 0.8): F = np.pi*np.sqrt(Rm)/(1 - Rm) rows.append((f"Ex. 2: finesse and mode width, R = {Rm}", f"F = {F:.1f}, δν = {dnu2/F/1e9:.2f} GHz = {dl2/F*1e12:.1f} pm")) pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["quantity", "value"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The conclusion of the live script, "the spectral width depends greatly on the mirror reflectances", holds for a **passive** cavity. The panel below shows what gain adds. A wave makes many round trips; with single-pass gain $e^{(g-\alpha_s)L}$ each round trip multiplies it by $R_1R_2e^{2(g-\alpha_s)L}$. As $g\to g_{th}$ this factor approaches 1, the transmission peaks diverge and their width collapses. A laser is a Fabry–Perot amplifier pushed to the point where it needs no input. ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof fp = Inputs.form({ R: Inputs.range([0.05, 0.99], {value: 0.32, step: 0.01, label: "facet reflectance R₁ = R₂"}), L: Inputs.range([50, 1000], {value: 250, step: 10, label: "cavity length L (µm)"}), n: Inputs.range([1, 4], {value: 3.6, step: 0.05, label: "refractive index n"}), frac: Inputs.range([0, 0.999], {value: 0.0, step: 0.001, label: "net gain (g − α_s)/(mirror loss)"}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false fpOut = { const c = 299792458, L = fp.L*1e-6, fsr = c/(2*fp.n*L), mir = Math.log(1/(fp.R*fp.R))/(2*L); const Gs = Math.exp(fp.frac*mir*L), rr = fp.R*Gs, data = []; for (let i = 0; i <= 1500; i++) { const dnu = -1.6*fsr + 3.2*fsr*i/1500, phi = Math.PI*dnu/fsr; data.push({f: dnu/1e9, T: (1 - fp.R)**2*Gs/((1 - rr)**2 + 4*rr*Math.sin(phi)**2)}); } const width = fsr/Math.PI*2*Math.asin((1 - rr)/(2*Math.sqrt(rr))); const peak = (1 - fp.R)**2*Gs/(1 - rr)**2; return {data, fsr, width, peak}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 280, x: {label: "frequency offset (GHz)"}, y: {label: "transmission", type: "log", grid: true}, marks: [Plot.line(fpOut.data, {x: "f", y: "T", stroke: "#2a78d6", strokeWidth: 2})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false html`
mode spacing ${(fpOut.fsr/1e9).toFixed(1)} GHz · peak transmission ${fpOut.peak.toPrecision(4)} · FWHM of each resonance ${fpOut.width > 1e9 ? (fpOut.width/1e9).toFixed(2) + " GHz" : (fpOut.width/1e6).toFixed(2) + " MHz"} (finesse ${(fpOut.fsr/fpOut.width).toFixed(1)})
` ``` ## Output versus pump rate (slide 68) The rate equations of a four-level laser, with $\beta$ the fraction of spontaneous emission that enters the lasing mode, show the threshold, the clamping of the inversion and the linear output: $$ \frac{dN}{dt}=R_p-\frac{N}{\tau_{sp}}-\frac{N\,S}{N_{th}\tau_{ph}},\qquad \frac{dS}{dt}=\frac{N\,S}{N_{th}\tau_{ph}}-\frac{S}{\tau_{ph}}+\beta\frac{N}{\tau_{sp}}. $$ ::: {#cell-fig-pump .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} Rp = np.logspace(-1, 1, 400) # pump in units of N_th/τ_sp fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8)) for beta, c in zip((1e-1, 1e-3, 1e-6), lz.PALETTE): # steady state (units N_th = τ_sp = τ_ph = 1 for N and rates; S in units of N_th τ_ph/τ_sp): # N(1 + S) = Rp and S(N − 1) + βN = 0 → S = βN/(1 − N); solve the quadratic for N a, b, cc = (1 - beta), -(1 + Rp), Rp # (1 − β)N² − (1 + Rp)N + Rp = 0 N = (-b - np.sqrt(b**2 - 4*a*cc))/(2*a) S = beta*N/(1 - N) ax[0].plot(Rp, N, color=c, label=f"β = {beta:g}") ax[1].loglog(Rp, S, color=c, label=f"β = {beta:g}") ax[0].plot(Rp, np.minimum(Rp, 1), ":", color=lz.INK2, lw=1.2, label="ideal") ax[0].set(xlabel="pump rate R_p/R_th", ylabel="inversion N/N_th"); ax[0].legend(fontsize=8) ax[1].set(xlabel="pump rate R_p/R_th", ylabel="photons in the mode S"); ax[1].legend(fontsize=8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Steady state of the rate equations versus pump rate (normalised to threshold, R_th = N_th/τ_sp). Left: inversion N/N_th, which clamps at 1 above threshold (slide 68). Right: photon number S (log scale) for three values of β. A smaller β gives a sharper threshold: the jump in S across threshold is about 1/β.](threshold_files/figure-html/fig-pump-output-1.png){#fig-pump width=1197 height=402} ::: ::: Gas and solid-state lasers have $\beta\sim10^{-8}$ to $10^{-10}$ and a razor-sharp threshold. Laser diodes have $\beta\sim10^{-4}$ to $10^{-5}$. Microcavity and nanolasers approach $\beta\to1$, the "thresholdless" laser, where the kink disappears and only photon statistics distinguish laser light from spontaneous emission. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Going further - **Optimum output coupling.** For a given small-signal gain $g_0$ and internal loss, too high an $R_1$ traps the light, too low a $R_1$ raises the threshold. Rigrod's analysis gives the output intensity $I_\text{out}\propto(1-R_1)\left[g_0L-\tfrac12\ln(1/R_1R_2)-\alpha_sL\right]/\ldots$; find the optimum $R_1$ numerically for the He–Ne laser ($g_0=0.15$ m⁻¹). - **Q factor and photon lifetime.** $Q=2\pi\nu_0\tau_{ph}$. Compute $Q$ for the presets of the calculator and compare with microring resonators ($Q\sim10^6$) and photonic-crystal cavities ($Q\sim10^6$, volume $\sim(\lambda/n)^3$). - **Spontaneous emission factor β.** Estimate $\beta$ for the He–Ne laser as the ratio of modes inside the lasing mode to all modes within the linewidth in the tube volume. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Complements - Kasap, sec. 4.6; Siegman, *Lasers*, ch. 11–13 (laser oscillation and output coupling); Svelto, ch. 7. - G. Björk and Y. Yamamoto, "Analysis of semiconductor microcavity lasers using rate equations", *IEEE J. Quantum Electron.* 27, 2386 (1991): the β-factor and thresholdless lasers. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. A He–Ne laser has $R_1=0.99$ instead of 0.95. Recompute $g_{th}$, $\tau_{ph}$ and the output power for the same photon concentration. Is the higher reflectance better? 2. With the calculator, find the minimum reflectance $R_1=R_2$ for which a 1 cm long gain medium with $g=0.5$ m⁻¹ can lase. 3. Show that $\tau_{ph}$ (exact) tends to $n/c\alpha_t$ when $\alpha_tL\ll1$. What is the error for a laser diode with $\alpha_tL=1.4$? 4. In the FP panel, what is the FWHM when the net gain reaches 99 % of the mirror loss? Compare with $1/2\pi\tau_{ph}$.
